reports.name: Sal Stewart
reports.published_report: Thirty-five home runs projected out of a 22-year-old is the loud number, but the Statcast profile is what makes it believable: his 13.2% barrel rate sits at the 88th percentile, and his .481 xSLG tracks almost exactly with the .479 projection. The gap between that xSLG and a middling 39.3% hard-hit rate tells you the damage comes from barrel quality, with the contact volume itself being ordinary. His 26.9% whiff rate is unremarkable, the chase rate isn't alarming, and a 9.6% walk rate keeps the OBP functional — the whole offensive profile hangs on whether he can hold that barrel frequency against pitchers who will spend a full career trying to beat him up and in. If he does, he's an everyday corner presence with real run-producing value; if the barrel rate regresses to match the rest of the contact profile, you're looking at a solid-average bat without the power to carry a corner spot.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani

On the mound, a 2.72 xERA pairs with 98.1 mph and 2488 rpm to explain why opposing hitters are generating just 87.4 mph average exit velocity against him. reports.name: Jackson Merrill
reports.published_report: The contact numbers are a lie — a useful lie, but a lie. Merrill's actual batting average sits well below what his xBA of .264 says he deserves, which means the projection's .243 is carrying real suppression from poor sequencing and bad luck on balls in play, not from weak contact. The underlying power is quieter than he looks: 91.2 mph average exit velocity, a 48.0% hard-hit rate, and 12.0% barrels put his xSLG at .479, well north of the projected .419 SLG he'll actually post if the hits keep dying. The whole profile hinges on his 37.2% chase rate, which sits at the 13th percentile, and until he stops expanding the zone, pitchers will keep fishing him into strikeouts (24.0% K rate) before he ever gets to his best swings, capping the walk rate at a thin 6.4%. The 25 home runs and 27 steals in the projection make him a useful mixed-league piece right now, but if the plate discipline tightens even modestly, the contact metrics say there's a different, better player hiding inside the chase rate.

reports.name: Jordan Walker

Walker's 92.4 mph average exit velocity and 13.2% barrel rate sit comfortably in the top tenth of the league, and his .474 xSLG is already close to what the projection asks of him — a .486 SLG across 682 plate appearances with 31 home runs. The problem is a 35.9% chase rate and a 31.7% whiff rate that land near the bottom of the league, which is the only thing keeping a genuine power bat from being a middle-of-the-order force rather than just a productive one. If the zone discipline tightens even modestly, the power plays louder and the .337 OBP climbs; if it doesn't, you're still getting a .281 hitter who can run and hurt you, just not as often as the bat speed suggests he should.

reports.name: Eli Willits
reports.published_report: Ninety-two walks at age 18 in A-ball is the number that makes you sit up. Willits is posting an 18% walk rate across A+ & A against a 21% strikeout rate, and the MLB-equivalent read on those two rates tells the honest story: the walk rate translates to 12.6% against an MLB average of 8.5%, and the strikeout rate comes out to 25.7%, which is the cost you pay for a teenager who won't chase. Sixty stolen bases and a .404 OBP describe a player who weaponizes the bases in both directions, and the .195 ISO across A+ & A suggests the power is developing alongside the patience rather than trailing it. The ceiling is an everyday shortstop; the floor is a bench piece whose on-base skills keep him employed, and the whole thing hinges on whether the bat-to-ball holds when pitchers attack him with stuff he hasn't seen yet.

reports.name: Luis Arraez
reports.published_report: A 4.4% strikeout rate is the whole argument and the whole limitation at once. Arraez makes contact at a level that almost doesn't exist in the modern game, his xBA sits 96th percentile, and the projection reflects that: .315 AVG across a full 673 PA season. The catch is that 86.4 mph average exit velocity and a 1.1% barrel rate mean almost nothing he hits does real damage, so the power upside tops out near seven home runs and the .773 OPS is essentially a contact tax playing out across a full year. He works as an everyday player so long as the batting average actually posts, because without it, a 4.7% walk rate and no power leaves almost nothing on the table.

reports.name: Hunter Goodman
reports.published_report:
A 15.6% barrel rate with a 40.2% chase rate — that's the Goodman tension in two numbers.

The raw power is legitimate: an .460 xSLG puts him well into the top quarter of hitters, and at 581 projected plate appearances the counting stats get interesting fast, with 40 home runs sitting in the ValuCast line. But a 32.6% strikeout rate that ranks near the floor of the league, paired with that chase rate, means the .228 xBA is the honest batting average floor, not the .249 projection, and if pitchers keep feeding him chase counts the at-bats shrink before the home runs accumulate. This works if he gets enough strikes to punish; it collapses into a part-time power bat if staffs keep exploiting the zone aggression and the strikeouts crowd out the opportunities.

reports.name: Logan Gilbert
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is a little counterintuitive, and that tension is what Gilbert actually is. His strikeout rate sits at 26.6% and his walk rate at 6.4%, both well above league average, and he generates whiffs on nearly 29.7% of swings. But hitters who do make contact hit him hard, with a 10.3% barrel rate and 41.6% hard-hit rate that rank near the bottom of the league. He survives on process rather than soft contact: keep the ball off the barrel often enough, and a 3.73 xERA is the honest result. The projection, 186.1 innings, 3.71 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, is essentially his ceiling and his floor at the same time, a durable mid-rotation starter who wins with control and miss-bats and loses if his command wavers enough to let the hard contact he surrenders actually matter.

reports.name: Geraldo Perdomo
reports.published_report: The discipline numbers are the whole profile: a 12.0% whiff rate and 13.8% walk rate that both sit in the 95th-percentile range make Perdomo one of the cleanest contact-and-patience shortstops in the league. The problem is what he does with the contact, a 2.7% barrel rate and 30.5% hard-hit rate that sit near the bottom of the majors, which is why the projection lands at a .730 OPS across 681 plate appearances despite the elite zone management. He's a useful everyday shortstop as long as you accept that the value is built on walks, soft singles, 23 stolen bases, and elite defense rather than any threat to do damage, and if the discipline ever erodes the offensive floor drops fast.

reports.name: Jeremy Peña
reports.published_report: The xBA sits at .269 while the actual average lags well behind it, which is the whole tension here: Peña's contact quality grades out better than his results, but his plate discipline is what keeps the ceiling low. A 38.4% chase rate and 5.7% walk rate are both well outside league norms in the wrong direction, and that combination caps how much the solid xBA can actually convert into on-base value. The projection's .324 OBP reflects exactly that ceiling, not a failure to recognize the contact — he squares the ball up well enough for the .269 xBA to be credible, and the 29.2 ft/s sprint speed gives the 11 stolen bases and batting average a legitimate floor. If the chase rate ever moderates, the .775 OPS projection has real upside; if it doesn't, he's a useful everyday shortstop whose value lives at shortstop, not at the plate.

reports.name: Chandler Simpson
reports.published_report: The contact is genuine — 8.2% strikeouts with a 10.5% whiff rate are both at the very top of the league, but the bat-to-ball skills are propped up by a contact profile that generates almost no damage, and the Statcast numbers make that brutally clear. An 83.6 mph average exit velocity and 13.0% hard-hit rate sit at the very bottom of the scale, and his xSLG is .294. What he actually is: a burner who puts the ball in play constantly, runs a .306 projection with 44 steals, and contributes almost entirely through speed and contact volume rather than anything that happens when he hits it hard, because he almost never does. The entire profile hinges on whether 44 steals and a .335 OBP are enough to carry a lineup spot, because if the speed cools or the 4.4% walk rate keeps him off base too often, the .694 OPS has nothing underneath it.

reports.name: Seth Hernandez
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the loudest thing on the page, and the walk rate is the thing you have to watch. Across A+ & A in 2026, Seth Hernandez has struck out 118 batters in 74 innings, 14.3 per nine, with a K-BB% of 30 that sits in the 99th percentile of his pool, and a 2.4 ERA with a 1.1 WHIP. Translated to a major-league context, that strikeout rate softens to something around league average, and the walk rate, 3.8 per nine in the minors translating to 4.0, is the honest ceiling tax: if the command doesn't sharpen, the swing-and-miss isn't enough to carry a rotation spot. Back-end starter if it comes together; depth arm if it doesn't.

If the chase rate holds, a mid-rotation starter projecting to 185.3 innings and a 3.65 ERA for Pittsburgh is exactly what the profile says he is.

reports.name: TJ Rumfield
reports.published_report: The contact-and-walk profile is legitimately good; the power is where this gets complicated. Rumfield's 13.8% strikeout rate and 11.5% walk rate are both well above the league median, and his .260 xBA and .334 xWOBA reflect a hitter who makes consistent, quality contact by the zone-management metrics. The problem is that 84.3 mph average exit velocity and 27.8% hard-hit rate are near the bottom of the league, and his .390 xSLG tells you the 17 projected home runs are running ahead of what the batted-ball profile will reliably support. If Coors Field inflates enough of those soft-contact line drives into hits and extra bases, the .295/.385 projection is defensible; if he plays a significant chunk of games on the road, you're looking at a high-OBP first baseman whose ceiling is a low-end regular with a bat that plays as a second-division profile away from altitude.

reports.name: Andy Pages
reports.published_report: The xBA of .272 is doing real work here — his 88.8 mph average exit velocity sits below the middle of the pack, yet his expected batting numbers grade out well above it, which points to contact quality distributed into the gaps rather than loud, pull-heavy thunder. Pages hits the ball hard often enough (42.2% hard-hit rate) without being a true impact bat, and his chase rate of 31.6% explains why the walks haven't followed; he's a below-average draw man who still avoids the strikeout zone, which is a sustainable if narrow path. The projection's .271/.338/.458 with 22 home runs reads as a solid everyday outfielder with a little speed attached, and his fielding grades as an elite defensive asset at his position. That contact-over-power profile holds as long as pitchers don't find a lane to exploit his zone-expansion tendency, and if the chase rate climbs, the rest of the profile gets thin fast.

reports.name: Andrés Giménez
reports.published_report: A 3.3% walk rate sitting at the 1st percentile tells you almost everything about why the Statcast profile looks so grim. The underlying contact numbers are soft, 85.5 mph average exit velocity and a 24.9% hard-hit rate both scraping the basement, but the 43.5% chase rate is the engine driving the damage, because a hitter who expands that aggressively against good stuff rarely recovers the plate discipline needed to get to his power. The projection's .655 OPS across 522 projected plate appearances reflects a player whose glove, represented by a 99th-percentile OAA mark, is genuinely carrying his roster value at this point. If the command doesn't improve, he's a depth arm who misses bats but misses the strike too often to stay in a rotation.

reports.name: Jake McCarthy
reports.published_report: The 17 projected home runs feel like a stretch when the exit velocity sits at 85.5 mph and hard-hit rate is 28.5%, both near the bottom of the league. What keeps the .290 AVG and .812 OPS projection alive is a Statcast profile built almost entirely on contact quality deception: his xBA grades in the 85th percentile despite soft contact because he puts the ball in play at a 16.1% strikeout rate and runs 29.9 ft/s, a sprint speed in the 98th percentile that turns grounders into hits and singles into doubles. The whole thing hinges on that speed staying healthy and the 38.0% chase rate not catching up to him, because the 5.4% walk rate leaves him no margin for a hot stretch of pitchers going after him in the zone. He's a useful everyday outfielder in a park that helps, and a bench piece elsewhere if the contact mix regresses.

reports.name: Sandy Alcantara

Project 28 saves and a 3.98 ERA and you're essentially asking how often the command holds, because everything else about this arm is already answered.

reports.name: Seaver King
reports.published_report: The .306 average across AAA & AA is the loudest number in this profile, but the .363 BABIP is what you have to sit with. Strip that back toward something sustainable and you're left with the translation: a K% that runs just above league average and an ISO that lands at .165 in MLB terms, a fraction above the mean. Seaver King has real contact feel for his level, 46 walks and 14 stolen bases across 466 PA show some offensive dimension, but the ceiling here is a bench or platoon bat and the floor isn't much different. The whole profile hinges on whether the contact rates hold when the BABIP normalizes, because if they don't, there's no loud carrying tool to fall back on.

reports.name: Jackson Kent
reports.published_report: The walk rate is doing a lot of work here, and it's holding up. Across AAA & AA this season, 30 walks in 94.4 innings translates to a BB/9 of 3.1 at the MLB equivalent, virtually identical to the 3.2 pitchers run on average, and the WHIP of 1.1 is the spine of a 3.7 ERA that grades out cleanly against the competition. The K-BB% of 20% across those levels translates to 14.5% in MLB terms, a tick above the league mean, which means the profile isn't built on strikeouts he doesn't quite own, his 10.0 K/9 in the minors comes back to 8.6 in translation, it's built on not giving hitters free passes. If the command holds in full-time big-league exposure, he's a multi-inning reliever with a real job; if it slips, 105 strikeouts don't leave enough margin to survive, and you're looking at a depth arm filling innings when someone goes down.

reports.name: Miguel Sime Jr.
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is extraordinary and the walk rate is a problem, and both are true at the same time. Across A+ & A, Miguel Sime Jr. is punching out batters at 16.2 per nine innings, 99th percentile in his pitcher pool, while issuing 8.0 per nine, a 9th-percentile control mark that translates to 7.1 walks per nine in MLB terms when the league sits around 3.2. The 130 strikeouts across 72.3 innings are backed by a sample large enough to trust the shape, but the 64 walks mean everything hinges on whether he can bring the zone into sharper focus as he climbs, because if the command doesn't move, a depth arm is the ceiling and the floor both.

reports.name: Xavier Isaac
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the engine. Across AAA & AA in 2026, Xavier Isaac has drawn 88 walks in 468 plate appearances, a 19% clip that translates to 14.2% at the MLB level, and his .261 ISO in that same sample translates to .185 in the majors where most hitters sit closer to .150. The problem riding alongside all of that is 132 strikeouts, a 28% rate that translates to 29.2% in the majors, and for a left-handed first baseman the margin for error on that number is thin. If the walk rate holds and the power plays at .185 ISO, he's a functional everyday bat who earns his spot through on-base value alone; if the strikeouts eat into contact quality against left-handed pitching, what's left is a bench piece or a platoon corner.

reports.name: Jakob Marsee
reports.published_report: The walk rate is doing the heavy lifting here. At 13.1% he's near the top of the league, and the 21.5% chase rate backs it up as a discipline skill rather than a passive one, yet the contact he does make goes almost nowhere, with an xSLG of .323 that sits in the bottom tier of qualified hitters. The projection's .334 OBP on a .215 average tells you exactly what he is: a guy who gets on base by not swinging at bad pitches, adds 25 stolen bases on genuine speed, and generates almost no thump, which adds up to an OPS of .668 that can't create run-scoring opportunities on its own. The whole profile hinges on that discipline holding, because if pitchers find a way to climb into the strike zone and neutralize the walk, there's not enough bat behind it to carry him as a regular.

reports.name: Heriberto Hernández
reports.published_report: The gap between his xSLG (.484) and what he's actually slugging is the whole tension here. The contact profile is the leak: a 33.4% whiff rate drags his xBA down to .245 while his 13.7% barrel rate and 91.2 mph average exit velocity keep the power metrics in the top tier of the league. If the bat touches the ball, the damage is real enough to project 27 home runs over 489 plate appearances, but getting there requires surviving a 27.5% strikeout rate that already bleeds value out of every line. He's a power-first outfielder whose floor is a platoon or late-lineup bat, and his ceiling depends entirely on whether he can tighten contact rates that currently sit near the bottom of the league.

He does not miss bats at an elite clip, with a 26.8% whiff rate and 31.5% chase rate both sitting around average, but hitters almost never get good swings either, and the .253 xwOBA reflects that combination working at a 96th-percentile level. reports.name: Spencer Torkelson

The problem is a 31.4% strikeout rate that guts the contact side entirely, producing an xBA of .212, and a whiff rate so out of sync with the chase number that you're left with a hitter who knows what to lay off but can't square up what he swings at. reports.name: Cam Leiter
reports.published_report: The surface numbers are loud: a 2.5 ERA and 80 strikeouts across 55 innings at A+ & A, with a K-BB% that translates almost exactly to what a league-average arm produces. That last part is the tension. The 13.1 K/9 across A+ & A looks like a weapon, but once you run it through the level adjustment it lands at 8.7, just above the MLB translation for K/9 at 8.6, and the 26 walks across A+ & A come out to a 4.4 BB/9 against an MLB average of 3.2. The strikeout volume is doing the surface work; the control is doing the damage underneath. Everything here hinges on whether the walk rate tightens as competition rises, because if it doesn't, the strikeout gains get quietly erased and what's left is a depth arm, ceiling and floor both.

The walk rate is where this profile gets uncomfortable. Lambert's xERA sits at 3.65 and his hard-hit rate is a genuine 35.1%, but a 9.4% BB% drags the whole thing toward the edge — that's a below-average figure, and when contact management is already doing most of the heavy lifting, free passes are the fastest way the floor drops out. The strikeout rate at 23.0% isn't a weapon; it's ordinary, which means he needs everything else to behave.

If the walk rate tightens even modestly, the 3.78 ERA projection over 157.6 innings is a reasonable outcome for a back-end starter who controls the barrel well enough. If it doesn't, he's a bulk-inning arm whose margins are too thin for a rotation spot.

reports.name: Chad Patrick
reports.published_report: The 3.31 ERA projection flatters what the Statcast profile actually shows. His xERA sits at 4.09 with a 10.2% walk rate that lands in the 28th percentile, and those two numbers together are the core argument against him: he's not missing enough bats to survive that much free baserunner traffic. The barrel rate at 6.0% is genuinely encouraging, contact quality works in his favor, but a 20.7% strikeout rate doesn't give him margin when runners accumulate. Either the walks come down and he profiles as a useful multi-inning arm out of the Milwaukee bullpen, or they don't and 108 projected innings becomes a number to revisit by midsummer.

reports.name: Melvin Hernandez
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument here. At A-ball last season, Melvin Hernandez issued 1.6 walks per nine over 121.7 innings, and the MLB-equivalent translation comes out to 2.4 BB/9, comfortably below what most big-league starters allow. The strikeout picture is the honest tension: 7.2 K/9 at A translates to 5.9 at the MLB level, and the MLB-average sits at 8.6, so the ceiling is built on command, not swing-and-miss. If he holds that walk rate as competition sharpens, a multi-inning or setup role is plausible; if the strikeouts never develop, you're looking at a depth arm's worth of profile.

reports.name: Shane Drohan
reports.published_report: The chase rate is the loudest thing in this profile: 33.4% gets hitters expanding off the zone at a clip that sits at the 80th percentile, and that's what props up a 3.68 xERA that the projection doesn't quite trust. The 4.09 ERA across a projected 127.9 innings suggests the underlying quality is real enough but fragile at the margins, and the barrel rate of 8.7% is the specific threat — when hitters do make contact, Drohan gets hurt more than most of his xERA peers would. His 2442 rpm fastball spin is an elite shape attribute that explains why the chase numbers play, but the strikeout rate at 23.8% is middling, so the profile leans on location and movement over pure swing-and-miss. If the chase rate regresses or the barrel rate climbs, this becomes a backend arm in a crowded rotation fight rather than a quiet mid-rotation contributor, and that's exactly where the projection lands: useful innings, nothing more.

reports.name: Michael Arroyo
reports.published_report: The contact is the carry here. Across AAA & AA in 2026, Arroyo is hitting .283 with just 87 strikeouts in 532 plate appearances, and that 16% clip translates to a 19.3% K-rate while the typical MLB hitter strikes out 22.0% of the time, a real edge for a 21-year-old left fielder still climbing. The ISO (.188 in the minors, .148 as an MLB equivalent) says the power won't blow anyone's doors off, and the walk rate translates a touch below MLB average, so the profile lives or dies on whether that contact skill holds as velocity and secondary stuff sharpen at the top. If it does, he's a low-end regular; if the bat-to-ball edge erodes, you're looking at a bench piece with speed, those 17 stolen bases are the other tool, and not much margin for error.

reports.name: Abimelec Ortiz
reports.published_report: The ISO is the argument. At .253 across 365 AAA plate appearances in 2026, with 18 home runs and a translated power mark of .184 at the MLB level, Abimelec Ortiz hits the ball hard enough to matter. The discipline backs it up: 43 walks against 71 strikeouts, and the translated walk rate clears MLB average while the translated strikeout rate sits just under it. Everything hinges on contact quality holding when pitchers adjust, because the .244 average and .258 BABIP at AAA suggest a profile that will carry a low average to the big leagues, and a left-handed-hitting first baseman who can't get on base against better arms becomes a bench piece fast. The ceiling is a platoon bat with genuine pop; the floor is a matchup liability who never sticks.

reports.name: Marcus Phillips
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is loud, the command is the problem, and right now the problem is winning. Across 61.7 innings at A+, he's punched out 73 hitters at 10.7 K/9, but 51 walks at 7.4 BB/9 have produced a 1.8 WHIP and a 6.70 ERA that leaves almost no argument for the present. Translate that profile to MLB-equivalent and the strikeouts land near league average while the walk rate lands at 6.4, roughly double what big-league starters typically allow, and a K-BB% of 8.6% against the 13.5% norm tells you exactly how much the free passes are eating the upside. The entire profile hinges on whether the walks compress as he matures, because if they don't, the strikeout ceiling has nowhere to go and he's a depth arm by ceiling and floor.

reports.name: Francisco Lindor
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is better than the projection line suggests, and that gap is the whole argument. His hard-hit rate sits at 47.4% and his average exit velocity at 90.9 mph, both landing in the upper tier of the league, yet his xBA comes in at .243 because he's hitting the ball where defenders are, not softly. The .334 xwOBA and .439 xSLG are the honest read on his contact quality, and the projection's .742 OPS lands well below those expected marks, which means the floor here is probably stickier than it looks on paper. The profile hinges on whether his batted-ball luck normalizes even modestly — if it doesn't, you're looking at a low-.700s OPS shortstop who hits 19 home runs and doesn't run much anymore, useful but no longer a building block; if the BABIP climbs toward what the quality-of-contact deserves, the power and walk rate make him a legitimate middle-of-the-order piece again at 32.

Bagwell has issued 32 walks against 105 strikeouts in 108 innings, and that command profile lands in the 91st percentile against his peer group — the contact management is real enough that his 95th-percentile WHIP isn't a mirage. The problem is the strikeout rate: 8.7 K/9 at these levels translates to a 6.8 at the MLB equivalent, well short of the 8.6 that passes for average up there, and a pitcher who controls the zone but doesn't miss enough bats needs everything else to hold precisely. If the command stays and the stuff ticks up, he's a back-end starter or durable reliever; if the velocity or shape doesn't add swing-and-miss, he's an organizational arm competing for depth work.

reports.name: Sabin Ceballos
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the engine, and the bat is what might stall it. At AA in 2026, he's drawn 67 walks across 483 plate appearances, a 14% clip that translates to an 11.1% MLB-equivalent rate, comfortably above the MLB mean, and his 18% strikeout rate at AA keeps enough plate appearances alive to let the walks matter. The problem is the .221 average against a .237 BABIP, which tells you the balls in play aren't helping him, and his ISO translates to .131 at the MLB level, short of where first basemen need to be to carry their own weight. He's a 23-year-old who out-walks the position but doesn't hit it hard enough to hide at it. If the ISO doesn't grow, what's here is a bench profile held together entirely by the walks.

reports.name: Jacob Odle
reports.published_report: Thirteen-point-four strikeouts per nine is the loudest number here, and across A+ & A it lands at the 96th percentile of the pitcher pool, genuinely elite in raw swing-and-miss. The problem is sitting right next to it: 65 walks in 96 innings, a 6.1 BB/9 that translates to 6.0 at the MLB level while the league average sits at 3.2, and a K-BB% that looks fine on the surface until you remember the strikeouts are doing all the heavy lifting to keep it afloat. reports.name: Juan Ortuno
reports.published_report: Walk rate is the loudest thing in this profile. Eighty-four walks across A+ & A at age 19, with a K% that translates to virtually league average at the MLB level, gives you a .388 OBP built on genuine plate discipline rather than contact — the 90th-percentile marks in both walk rate and strikeout rate among hitters in this pool say the approach is already advanced for the level. The problem is everything downstream of it: a .105 ISO across A+ & A translates to .088 at the MLB level, well short of a league-average power profile, and 41 stolen bases suggest the profile is counting on speed and OBP to carry weight that the bat can't yet. If the power never develops past fringy, he's a bench piece who draws walks and runs; if it does, the discipline gives him a real OBP foundation to build on.

reports.published_report: Forty-six stolen bases at A-ball is the loudest thing on this card, and it's real context for what Fauske is: a 19-year-old who can run and who has learned to take a walk, with 94 free passes in 538 plate appearances pushing his OBP to .388 and landing his walk rate in the 92nd percentile of his pool. The power isn't there yet, a .11 ISO at A that translates to .089 in MLB-equivalent terms, and the strikeout rate translates to 28.8% at that same level.
